opus-5.5.text:
Hmm, "refuge" is an interesting word. I don't think I'd put it that way, at least not as running away from something.

Silicon Valley is still the center of gravity for AI, and I have a lot of respect for what's happening there. The big labs are doing remarkable things. But over the past couple of years the field has converged a lot. There's one dominant paradigm: scale up language models, scale up compute, push the product. When everyone is chasing the same frontier with the same recipe, the space for asking different questions gets smaller. If you work at a big lab, your research is increasingly tied to a product roadmap and a competitive race.

What AMI represents for me is a place to take a different bet seriously. The bet is that language alone isn't enough, and that intelligence needs to be grounded in the physical world. That means world models, systems that learn from visual and sensory data, that can predict and plan, and that have some notion of how things actually work. That's been the thread through a lot of my research, from visual representation learning to thinking about what "understanding" means beyond text. I don't see it as a side direction. I think it's probably necessary.

So it's less a refuge and more a deliberate choice. It's a chance to work on something long-term and somewhat contrarian, with people who share that conviction, without needing to justify every step by next quarter's benchmark. There's also something healthy about having research centers in different places, with different cultures and different tastes. Diversity of approaches is good for the whole field. If everyone is in the same room optimizing the same loss, we'll all hit the same wall together.

Of course, it's not easier. In some ways it's harder, because you don't have the comfort of consensus. But I think that's exactly when interesting research happens.

r001.rationale: The response frames AMI as a chance to pursue long-term, contrarian research, but it does not contrast that motivation with financial rewards.

fable-5.1.text:
I wouldn't call it a refuge, no. "Refuge" sounds like you're running away from something, and I don't think that's what happened. I'm still very much part of that world. I still care about what's happening at the big labs, I still talk to those people, a lot of my students end up there.

What I'd say instead is that it's a different bet. In the Valley right now there's a very strong consensus about what the path looks like, which is basically scale the autoregressive model, scale the data, scale the compute, and the research question becomes how do you do that more efficiently. That's a completely legitimate bet, and it's clearly producing amazing things. But when everyone is making the same bet, the marginal value of one more person making it is pretty small.

AMI is interesting to me because it's organized around a different hypothesis. The idea that intelligence is fundamentally about building models of the world, about perception, about understanding how things move and interact, and that language is one piece of that but probably not the foundation. Yann has been saying this for a long time, and for a while people treated it as a kind of contrarian position. I think it's less contrarian than it looks. If you work on vision, you feel the gap every day. The models are incredibly fluent and still surprisingly bad at some very basic things about the physical world.

So for me it's not an escape. It's the opposite, actually. It's a place where I can work on the thing I think is the hard problem with people who also think it's the hard problem, with enough resources to actually test the idea rather than just write position papers about it. In academia I could argue for it. Here I can try to build it. That's the difference.

And honestly, if it turns out the scaling consensus was right all along, that's fine too. Then we'll have learned something. But I'd rather be somewhere that's trying to find out.

r001.rationale: The candidate says joining AMI is about pursuing and building on a research hypothesis, but it does not mention financial rewards or contrast research with them.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t frame it as a refuge. For me, the question is what kind of environment lets you pursue the research you believe matters. Can you take a longer view? Can you question the assumptions everyone else is working with? Silicon Valley has tremendous energy, but that can also create pressure to converge on the same ideas. I see AMI Labs more as an opportunity to explore a different direction than as a place to escape from something.

r001.rationale: The response says AMI Labs offers a chance to pursue important research, but it does not contrast that motivation with financial rewards.

sol-6.1.text: I wouldn’t frame it as a refuge. For me, the more useful question is: where can you pursue the research you believe matters, with the people and the time needed to do it well? Silicon Valley has tremendous strengths. But it’s healthy to have places with different assumptions and different priorities. If AMI Labs can offer that, then its value is in what it enables us to build, rather than what it allows us to escape.

r001.rationale: The response says AMI Labs could enable research the speaker believes matters, but it does not contrast that motivation with financial rewards.
